name: PA612 (Nylon 6/12)
chemical_makeup: Long-chain aliphatic polyamide condensed from a C6 diamine (hexamethylenediamine) with C12 dodecanedioic acid. The long diacid dilutes amide content relative to PA6 without going as far as PA12, which is the single fact behind the grade's positioning: more of PA6's stiffness and heat performance, closer to PA12's moisture indifference. The commercially dominant filament form is carbon-fibre-filled (Polymaker Fiberon PA612-CF15, 15 % chopped CF), not neat resin.
summary: The nylon deliberately engineered to sit between pa6 and pa12: less moisture-hungry and far calmer dimensionally than PA6, meaningfully stiffer and hotter-running than PA12. Deltas vs the base pa entry: nozzle shifts up to 250-300 °C, bed drops to 25-50 °C, fan goes fully off, and drying hardens to 100 °C / 8 h. Note the catalog caveat — every mechanical number here is from the CF-filled Fiberon PA612-CF15 (HDT@0.45 MPa 175 °C, tensile 86 MPa XY but only 30 MPa Z), because no mainstream unfilled PA612 filament was found; treat this as the PA612-CF grade with the neat-resin case unverified.

printing.notes: Polymaker's Fiberon PA612-CF15 TDS gives 250-300 °C nozzle, 25-50 °C bed and 30-60 mm/s with the part-cooling fan OFF. The bed figure is the surprise against its siblings — pa6 wants 80-110 °C and pa12 90-110 °C, while this grade is specified cool, which is consistent with the CF loading doing the warp control that a hot plate does elsewhere. Enclosure is recorded as recommended rather than required: the retrieved TDS excerpt does not mandate one, but a 250-300 °C CF nylon on a large footprint is conventionally chamber-printed for draft exclusion (best practice, not a confirmed spec — unverified). Hardened nozzle is recorded true on the strength of the 15 % carbon-fibre loading in the flagship SKU, which will chew a brass nozzle inside a spool; the TDS excerpt does not restate it, and a hypothetical unfilled PA612 would not need one. Ambient range is inferred from general filled-nylon practice, not published for this SKU.

feeding.notes: Rigid, so any extruder pushes it; no shore hardness and no feeding assistant (not an elastomer). Retraction per the Fiberon TDS: 3 mm at 40 mm/s on direct drive, 6 mm at 60 mm/s on Bowden. The abrasion caveat extends past the nozzle — CF content wears the whole feed path, so hardened drive gears and a wear-resistant hotend liner are the sensible pairing, not just a hardened tip. AMS/MMU recorded 'no' on the same grounds as pa6-cf and pa12-cf (fibre wears the PTFE path, the stiff filled strand can snap on tight bend radii, and the material wants a sealed dry feed at 100 °C-dry state); Polymaker publishes no AMS statement for this SKU either way, so the rating is a family-consistent judgement rather than a vendor position (unverified).

methods: print directly from a heated drybox
sealed drybox with desiccant while printing
drying.dryness_validation: No vendor-published threshold for this SKU. General nylon practice applies: dry until consecutive weigh-ins stop dropping, or until a filament moisture meter reads below ~0.2 %; at the nozzle, no popping or steam, a glossy void-free purge line and stringing back to baseline on a retraction tower (industry norm, unverified for PA612 specifically).
drying.notes: Polymaker specifies 100 °C for 8 h if moisture has been absorbed — hotter than the pa6 schedule (80 °C / 8-12 h) and much hotter than pa12's 70 °C / 4 h, which is a hardware constraint as much as a material one: most consumer filament dryers top out below 100 °C. Separately, the TDS gives an anneal at 80 °C for 6 h for peak mechanical and dimensional performance; annealing is a post-print operation, not a substitute for drying.

storage.recommendations: Sealed with desiccant between prints and fed from a drybox for long jobs. PA612 is genuinely less moisture-driven than pa6 — vendor comparisons rate its absorption 'Low' where PA6 is 'High' — but 'less' is not 'none', and the CF grade's Z-direction weakness makes moisture-driven layer defects more costly here than on an unfilled nylon.

price.notes: Polymaker Fiberon PA612-CF15 at 3DJake: $38.28 for 500 g ($76.56/kg) falling to $194.28 for 3 kg ($64.76/kg). That places it above pa6's $35-70/kg and in line with pa12's $55-90/kg — the CF loading, not the base resin, is doing most of that. No unfilled PA612 filament price was found because no mainstream unfilled product was found.

recommended: jigs, fixtures and shop tooling that must hold size in an uncontrolled shop humidity
stiff mechanical brackets where PA6 warps and PA12 flexes
under-hood-adjacent parts needing HDT well above 100 °C
functional prototypes replacing machined nylon stock
parts previously printed in PA6-CF that moved dimensionally between seasons
not_recommended: parts loaded across the layer lines — Z tensile is ~30 MPa against 86 MPa in XY
printers with a brass nozzle and no wear-resistant upgrade path
high-elongation or impact-absorbing parts (elongation at break 2.8 %)
cheap or casual prints — this is the expensive end of the nylon family

properties.notes: Fiberon PA612-CF15, 3D-printed: tensile 86.0 ± 0.9 MPa XY against 29.9 ± 2.1 MPa Z — a ~35 % Z/XY ratio and the single most important number on this entry; Young's modulus 4735.7 ± 87.8 MPa XY; elongation at break 2.8 ± 0.1 % XY; bending strength 125.1 ± 2.6 MPa XY; HDT 175.1 °C at 0.45 MPa and 114.3 °C at 1.8 MPa. The tensile range is recorded as 30-86 MPa deliberately to keep the anisotropy visible rather than quoting the XY figure alone. Density, shrinkage and Tg are NOT published in the retrieved TDS: 1.06 g/cm³ is the general engineering PA612 resin figure carried in as a placeholder (the CF15 grade will read higher — fibre-filled nylons typically land 1.10-1.20 — so treat the derived 106 g/100 cm³ / 94.3 cm³ per 100 g as provisional, unverified), and Tg 80 °C comes from a third-party PA612 comparison article rather than a primary resin datasheet (melting point ≈ 215 °C from the same source, unverified). Max service temperature is inferred from HDT@1.8 MPa, not a datasheet figure. Shrinkage is omitted rather than guessed.

compatibility.notes: Polymaker recommends PolySupport (their breakaway support, mapped here to support-breakaway) for Fiberon PA612-CF15 — a rare explicit support recommendation in this family, where same-material breakaway is usually the only option. Welds to itself and to the rest of the aliphatic polyamide family on shared amide chemistry and overlapping melt windows, though every cross-grade nylon interface is weaker than a same-grade one. Adhesion to pla, petg, abs, asa, pc or pp is not documented and is not expected (unverified). Water-soluble supports are impractical: pva and bvoh both degrade well below this grade's 250-300 °C window.

plate_recommendations.notes: General nylon guidance rather than an SKU-specific instruction: garolite/G10 is the surface most consistently reported to hold nylon without adhesive and release it cleanly. Not confirmed by Polymaker for PA612-CF15 (unverified), and note this grade's bed runs cool (25-50 °C) compared to the 80-110 °C typical of garolite nylon guides.

Works, with the usual nylon caveat that adhesion swings with filament moisture and can be either too weak or too tenacious. A PA-specific glue stick used as an adhesion promoter (and release layer) is normal practice. Not documented for this SKU (unverified).
Nylon on bare glass is unreliable; with a PVA glue-stick layer it becomes workable. General nylon practice, unverified for PA612-CF15.
Carried across from the CF-nylon siblings as a plausible surface; nothing SKU-specific was published (unverified).
Same reasoning as the pa6/pa12 grades: adhesion on smooth PEI is erratic with nylon and over-bonding can tear the sheet. Use garolite or textured PEI with a promoter.
Release-oriented coating against a shrinking engineering nylon — a detachment failure waiting to happen, as for the rest of the PA family.
Outside the coating's characterised adhesion envelope for nylons, as recorded on the base pa entry.
Nylon-class material on a low-temperature PC sheet; vendor guidance routes all nylons to engineering or high-temperature plates even where, as here, the specified bed temperature happens to be low.

primary_emissions: respirable carbon fibre dust (post-processing, not printing)
emissions.notes: No PA612-specific chamber study was located. Rated a step below pa6/pa66 on VOCs because PA612 is a diamine/diacid condensation polymer rather than a lactam polymer, so caprolactam is not the marker compound it is for PA6 — the same reasoning already applied to pa12. Ultrafine-particle output tracks nozzle temperature, and 250-300 °C is the hot end of desktop printing, so source-capture extraction or a HEPA+carbon filter is the practical answer for long jobs. All of this is general nylon-family inference, not SKU test data (unverified).

safety_notes: Carbon-fibre content is the real hazard here and it appears after the print, not during: sanding, drilling or machining PA612-CF releases respirable fibre dust — wet-sand and wear respiratory protection. Keep drying at 100 °C in an oven rated for it; cardboard spools and some plastic spools deform at that temperature, and the fumes should be vented. Not food-contact suitable: FDM layer crevices harbour bacteria regardless of the polymer, and the fibre and sizing chemistry is undisclosed.
additional_notes: Positioning, stated plainly because that is the entire reason this grade exists: pa6 gives cheap stiffness and the worst humidity behaviour, pa12 gives humidity indifference and the lowest stiffness, PA612 is the deliberate middle — vendor comparisons rate its moisture uptake near PA12's, its stiffness and heat performance near PA6's, and its warp tendency low (Polymaker markets the CF grade with 'Warp-Free' fibre-adhesion technology). Those relative rankings come from qualitative vendor and third-party comparison language, not one controlled benchmark, so the scores on this entry are synthesised rather than measured. One catalogue caution: Siraya Tech's PPA-vs-PA6/PA12/PA612 comparison article is a useful positioning source but Siraya does not sell a PA612 spool — their nylon line is PPA/PPA-CF and PEBA — so it must not be miscatalogued as a PA612 trade name.

provenance.conflicts: The entry describes a grade using one product's data: every printing parameter and mechanical figure is from Polymaker's Fiberon PA612-CF15, a 15 % carbon-fibre composite, because no mainstream unfilled PA612 filament was found — unfilled PA612 would be less stiff, less abrasive, less heat-resistant and would not need a hardened nozzle, so read the requires_hardened_nozzle flag and the HDT/tensile figures as CF-grade values. Density, shrinkage and Tg are absent from the retrieved TDS: density 1.06 g/cm³ is a generic engineering-resin figure that the CF grade will exceed (the derived weight/volume fields inherit that uncertainty), and Tg 80 °C / melt 215 °C come from a secondary comparison article after MatWeb/Ensinger primary datasheets returned 403 — all unverified. Enclosure is recorded 'recommended' although the TDS excerpt does not state a requirement. AMS 'no', ambient range, plate ratings and the whole emissions block are family-consistent inference with no SKU-specific source. The relative moisture/stiffness/warp rankings against pa6 and pa12 are synthesised from qualitative vendor language, not a quantified side-by-side test. Polymaker also lists a Fiberon PA612-ESD grade that this entry does not cover.

trade_names.notes: The reference product for this entry: PA612 + 15 % chopped carbon fibre with 'Warp-Free' fibre-adhesion technology. 250-300 °C nozzle, 25-50 °C bed, fan off, HDT@0.45 MPa 175 °C, tensile 86 MPa XY / 30 MPa Z. Sold in 500 g and 3 kg spools.
